area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a forward slip burns off extra altitude without adding airspeed, and fly a forward slip to a landing to ACS standards, including the switch to a sideslip in a crosswind.
why: A slip lets you lose height fast without gaining speed, which helps when you are high, have no flaps, or must glide to a field after an engine failure [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

prereading.what: Intentional slips, sideslip vs. forward slip, slip limits, slip limitations, forward slip to a landing, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-12 to 9-15

prereading.what: Crosswind approach: crab vs. wing-low, round out, touchdown, rollout, crosswind common errors, turbulent air approach.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-15 to 9-20

prereading.what: Stabilized approach, aiming point, runway shape, go-around criteria.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-4 to 9-6

prereading.what: Energy management: altitude and airspeed as energy; throttle and elevator roles.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 4, 4-1 to 4-4

warmup: You turn final 300 feet higher than you planned, power already at idle, and your airplane has no flaps. If you just push the nose down, what happens to your airspeed? What else could you do to come down faster?

key_terms.def: Flight where the bank is too steep for the rate of turn; the airplane moves partly sideways through the air [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
A slip used to lose altitude and steepen the descent without gaining airspeed; the nose points away from the flightpath [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
A slip where the nose stays lined up with the original path and the airplane moves sideways toward the low wing; used for crosswind landings [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Aileron one way, rudder the other. An intentional slip usually needs it throughout the maneuver [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
The point where full rudder is needed to hold heading; more bank would make the airplane turn [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Planning, watching and controlling altitude and airspeed as the airplane's total energy [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
The spot you are descending toward on a steady glide path; it does not seem to move in the windshield [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Stalling speed in the landing configuration [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

chunks.title: What a forward slip is, and when to use it

body.p: A slip happens when the bank is too steep for the rate of turn. Done on purpose, a slip lets you lose altitude without gaining airspeed, or adjust your ground track in a crosswind [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
In a slip the airplane flies partly sideways through the air. Drag goes way up, and because the wings are banked, less lift points up. So you come down fast without speeding up [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Forward slip
Sideslip
rows: Lose altitude, steepen descent, no extra speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Crosswind landing: keep aligned with centerline [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Lower a wing, enough opposite rudder to keep the original path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Lower a wing, just enough opposite rudder to stop a turn [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

bullets: You are too high on approach and need to come down without gaining speed.
Flaps are inoperative or not installed.
Forced landings, and clearing obstacles into confined areas.
Engine failure: you can start a slip faster than you can lower flaps, and you can take it out with no penalty. Raising flaps could cost you altitude.

callout.text: Forward slip = nose off to the side, track straight, come down. Sideslip = nose straight, wing into the wind, stay on centerline.

check.q: Why can you take out a slip "without penalty" but not always raise flaps?
check.a: Removing the slip just reduces the descent. Retracting flaps on approach can cause an unwanted loss of altitude [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Energy: why a slip is the right tool when high

body.p: Your airplane's total energy is altitude (potential energy) plus airspeed (kinetic energy) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. The throttle controls total energy. The elevator trades energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

Too high on final with power already at idle means too much total energy. If you only push the nose down, you trade altitude for airspeed: the energy is still there, now as extra speed. A slip adds a lot of drag, so it removes energy instead of moving it [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

bullets: "Higher and faster" or "lower and slower" = a total energy error. Fix with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]] (or, when already at idle, with drag, which can only remove energy [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]).
"Higher and slower" or "lower and faster" = wrong mix. Fix with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
In the slip, the steeper the bank, the steeper the descent. Control airspeed with the elevator [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

callout.text: Using power while trying to lose altitude in a slip works against you; it is a listed common error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

check.q: You are high on final, at idle, on target airspeed. Which box of the energy matrix are you in, and why is a slip a good fix?
check.a: Higher at desired airspeed = total energy high (box 4) [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. A slip adds drag and steepens the descent without increasing airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

chunks.title: Wind, air and runway effects on the approach

body.p: You land at the same indicated airspeed no matter the wind. What changes is your groundspeed at touchdown, and that changes landing distance a lot [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

head: Condition
Effect
rows: Wind changes gliding distance over the ground; correct with pitch and power [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]
Can cause an overshoot of final and a tempting skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Same IAS, higher TAS, longer landing; at 5,000 feet about 16 percent longer than sea level [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
At least 21 percent more landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Power-on approach, slightly faster; often normal speed plus half the gust factor [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]

body.p: Gust example from the AFH: normal speed 70 knots, gusts 15 knots, fly 77 knots. Speeds and flaps still follow the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

Wind shear is a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area. A headwind that turns into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance. A microburst on approach can force an airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

callout.text: A slip already means a high sink rate. Add a sudden loss of headwind close to the ground and you can run out of altitude fast. Be ready to take out the slip, add power, and go around [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

check.q: About how much does a 10-knot tailwind add to landing distance?

chunks.title: Crosswind: slip into the wind, then sideslip to touchdown

body.p: With a crosswind, lower the upwind wing so you bank into the wind. Slipping into the wind makes it easier to stay on your flightpath [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Slipping the same way the wind blows is a listed common error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Before the round out, change from the forward slip to a sideslip (wing-low). Use rudder to line the nose up with the runway, then use aileron bank just enough to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

bullets: Keep the upwind wing down through the round out. If you level the wings, you drift and touch down sideways [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Controls get weaker as you slow, so add more rudder and aileron as you flare [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Touch down on the upwind main wheel first; the other wheel settles as you slow [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
If nose-wheel steering is linked to the rudder, relax rudder as the nose-wheel touches so you don't swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On rollout, hold aileron into the wind, full into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

callout.text: Touching down while drifting puts side loads on the gear. In a tricycle-gear airplane that can tip it over. As little as 10 degrees of cornering angle makes a side load equal to half the supported weight [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
If full opposite rudder can't stop the turn with the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway. Use a better runway or another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

check.q: In a left crosswind, which wing do you lower in the forward slip?
check.a: The left (upwind) wing, banking into the wind [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

body.p: The AFH plans the whole pattern so a forward slip can be used on final. Flaps usually stay up [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Speeds, flap use and slip limits for your airplane come from the POH [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

bullets: 1. Downwind: fly parallel to the runway about 1/2 to 1 mile out at pattern altitude. Finish the before-landing checklist [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
2. Radio (non-towered): "On left/right downwind for runway XX" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. At a towered field, follow ATC.
3. Pick the touchdown point. Think about wind, surface, obstacles and your airplane's limits (ACS PA.IV.M.S4).
4. Abeam the landing point: power to idle and start down. If you aren't sinking fast enough, slip on downwind [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
5. Turn base with a coordinated turn. Judge your height. Still high? Keep slipping on base [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Call "On left/right base" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
6. Turn final with a coordinated turn [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Call "On final" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
7. On final: lower the wing (upwind wing if there is a crosswind), add opposite rudder to hold your track. More bank = steeper descent. Hold airspeed with the elevator [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
8. Adjust left or right of the track by changing aileron, even at full rudder [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].
9. To exit: level the wings and smoothly release rudder while setting normal glide pitch. Don't snap the rudder off [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
10. At the round out: take out the slip and land normally, or switch to a sideslip if there is a crosswind [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] (ACS PA.IV.M.S7).
11. Touch down on the centerline, no drift, nose aligned, then finish the after-landing checklist [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

callout.text: Your airspeed indicator may read wrong in a slip because of where the pitot tube and static vents are. Judge the slip by attitude, the sound of the air and the feel of the controls [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

Reached full rudder but still too high? Lowering the nose sinks you faster but adds speed, which also makes the rudder stronger. Raising the nose weakens the rudder, so reduce bank [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

check.q: Where does the AFH say to reduce power to idle in this maneuver?
check.a: When abeam the landing point on the downwind leg [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

body.p: A slip is a fix for being high, but it does not make a bad approach good. Pilots typically go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC. In a typical GA piston pattern, go around right away if the approach becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: Stable approach item (typical piston)
Guide
rows: +10/-5 KIAS of recommended landing speed (AFM, 1.3 VSO, or placard) [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Generally 500-1,000 fpm; if more than 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Track the centerline; bank normally 15 degrees or less once on final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Done before the approach (except landing checklist) [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

body.p: Watch the runway shape: too steep and it looks long and narrow; too shallow and it looks short and wide [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
Go-around: power first (full, smooth, carb heat off as applicable), then attitude (expect strong nose-up and left yaw; use forward pressure and right rudder), then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Two things delay go-arounds: landing expectancy ("it'll work out") and pride ("going around means I failed") [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Below what height should a typical GA piston pilot go around right away if the approach becomes unstable?

chunks.title: Slip hazards: fuel, flaps, airspeed, stall/spin

bullets: Fuel flowage: some airplanes limit slips by time or fuel quantity. Uncoordinated flight can push fuel to one side of a tank and starve the engine [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

Flaps: there may be recommendations or limits on slipping with flaps for aerodynamic reasons. Check the AFM/POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Flaps change downwash on the horizontal tail and the tail-down force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Airspeed: the indicator can be in error in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Reacting to it is a common error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Sink rate: the sideslip's extra drag and lost vertical lift can cause too much sink or too little airspeed [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

body.p: Stall in a slip vs. a skid: a slipping airplane that stalls shows very little of the yaw that turns a skidding stall into a spin. It may just roll toward wings level [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

The killer is the skid. A skidding cross-control stall is most likely in a poorly flown base-to-final turn. The airplane can roll inverted, the start of a spin. Near the ground, keep bank at or below 30 degrees, never skid to fix an overshoot, and go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Energy mistakes play a part in loss of control in flight, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents, the three most common fatal accident types [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Don't try to stretch a low approach with elevator alone; it can lead to a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

check.q: Why do some POHs limit how long you may slip?
check.a: To prevent fuel starvation from fuel being pushed to one side of a tank in uncoordinated flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

chunks.title: Traffic, wake, LAHSO, surface and distractions

body.p: Choose the runway, path and touchdown spot by your skill, the airplane's performance, the distance available and the wind (ACS PA.IV.M.R1). A slip steepens your descent, but you still need room to land and stop.

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Most midairs happen in good weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. Before turning final, make sure no one is already on final [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above its path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
After a larger aircraft's low approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate; the PIC may decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Not authorized for solo student pilots [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]].
On every final, verify the runway number and alignment; if in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Snow, ice or soft ground has a significant effect on landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Each 10 feet above the standard 50 feet adds about 200 feet of landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]. Finish the slip early enough to cross at the normal height.

body.p: Distractions: many start as a small problem that pulls attention from flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. In a slip you are busy with crossed controls, airspeed and the aiming point. Do checklists early, and when overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: Aviate first. If the slip, the traffic and the radio pile up, take out the slip and go around.

check.q: Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway, where do you touch down?
check.a: Beyond its touchdown point, staying at or above its flight path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

head: What the examiner checks
Standard
rows: Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point (ACS PA.IV.M.S8)
Proper pitch attitude, no side drift, longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS PA.IV.M.S8)
Aligned with the runway center/landing path (ACS PA.IV.M.S9)
Correlate the slip with the crosswind (slip into the wind, upwind wing low); transition to a sideslip before touchdown (ACS PA.IV.M.S7)

body.p: Common errors with forward slips to a landing [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]:

bullets: Bad pitch control, so poor airspeed control.
Reacting to wrong airspeed readings.
Using too much power while trying to lose altitude.
Slipping in the same direction as the crosswind.
Poor glidepath control.
Late switch to a sideslip in a crosswind.
Landing with the nose not parallel to the runway.
Landing off the centerline.

check.q: What is the ACS touchdown tolerance for this Task?
check.a: Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point (ACS PA.IV.M.S8).

scenario.title: High on a gusty, no-flap final
scenario.setup: You are practicing forward slips at a non-towered field, flaps up. Wind is 20 degrees off the runway from the left, gusting. A tailwind on base pushes you past the centerline, and you roll out on final high. You start a slip, the airspeed needle bounces, and another airplane calls a 2-mile final behind you.

questions.q: You overshot the turn to final. Should you add bottom rudder to swing the nose around?
questions.a: No. That sets up a skidding cross-control stall that can become a spin. Keep bank at or below 30 degrees and go around if needed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: Which wing do you lower for the slip?
questions.a: The left (upwind) wing, so you slip into the wind [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

questions.q: The airspeed needle bounces in the slip. What do you trust?
questions.a: Attitude, sound of the airflow and feel of the controls; the airspeed indicator may have error in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

questions.q: What speed would you fly if normal approach speed is 70 knots and gusts are 15 knots?
questions.a: About 77 knots (normal plus half the gust factor), unless the POH says otherwise [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

questions.q: At 250 feet AGL you are still high and fast. What now?
questions.a: Go around. In a typical GA piston pattern, go around right away if the approach becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Take out the slip, full power, pitch for climb, announce on CTAF.

questions.q: How do you keep the traffic behind you from becoming a hazard?
questions.a: Keep scanning and keep communicating your position in the pattern; see-and-avoid and good communication are key mitigations [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Use the before-landing checklist on downwind and the after-landing checklist once clear.
skills.practice: Say each item out loud on every pattern; finish it on downwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

skills.do: Make position calls (downwind, base, final) or follow ATC.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the calls with the runway number [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Plan a path from downwind to the touchdown spot that needs a slip, considering altitude, wind, terrain and obstacles.
skills.practice: Pull power at the abeam point, flaps up, and judge height on each leg [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

skills.do: Name and use a touchdown point that fits the wind, surface, obstacles and airplane.
skills.practice: Have your CFI pick a point each lap; call it before turning base.

skills.do: Fly downwind parallel to the runway at pattern altitude.
skills.practice: Hold about 1/2 to 1 mile out; correct for drift [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

skills.do: Set the configuration for a slip approach: usually flaps up, power idle, per the POH.
skills.practice: Brief POH slip and flap limits before flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

skills.do: Slip into the crosswind, then switch to a sideslip before touchdown.
skills.practice: At altitude, practice changing from a forward slip to a sideslip on a road line, then in the pattern [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

skills.do: Touch down at proper pitch, within 400 feet beyond or on the point, no drift, nose aligned over the centerline.
skills.practice: Remove the slip at the round out and hold the flare; debrief where you touched down.

skills.do: Keep the ground track on the centerline throughout.
skills.practice: Use aileron to move left or right of track while holding rudder [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a forward slip?
quiz.why: A forward slip dissipates altitude and increases descent rate without increasing airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: In a forward slip, what mainly controls the sink rate?
quiz.why: The amount of slip, and so the sink rate, is set by the bank angle; steeper bank, steeper descent [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: In a forward slip, you control airspeed mainly with:
quiz.why: The pilot controls airspeed using elevator control [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: With a crosswind from the right, you should:
options: Slip in whichever direction is comfortable
quiz.why: Lower the upwind wing so you bank into the wind [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Why might your airspeed indicator be unreliable in a slip?
options: Pitot tube and static vent location
quiz.why: Due to pitot tube and static vent location, some airspeed indicators have considerable error in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Why do some airplanes limit slip duration?
options: Fuel can be forced to one side of a tank, starving the engine
quiz.why: Limits prevent fuel starvation from fuel being forced to one side of a tank in uncoordinated flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: You hit full rudder but need to descend faster. Lowering the nose will:
quiz.why: Lowering the nose increases sink rate and airspeed, which also makes the rudder more effective [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: What is the ACS touchdown tolerance for a forward slip to a landing?
options: Within 400 feet beyond or on the point
Within 500 feet either side of the point
quiz.why: Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point (ACS PA.IV.M.S8).

takeaways: A forward slip removes energy with drag: down fast, no extra speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Bank sets sink rate; elevator holds airspeed; power normally at idle [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Slip into the wind, then switch to a sideslip before touchdown [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
Fly attitude, sound and feel; the airspeed indicator may lie in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Check the POH for slip limits with fuel and flaps [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Unstable below 300 feet AGL? Go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
cfi_notes: Have students practice entries and exits at altitude over a road first; then in the pattern with flaps up per the AFH setup [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

Students often fix a high final with the elevator alone and build speed; tie it to the energy matrix: pushing over from box 4 only moves them to box 8 (on altitude but fast; total energy still high) [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Watch for abrupt rudder release on exit, which swings the nose and adds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Examiners probe wind direction vs. slip direction and the late transition to a sideslip; both are AFH common errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Contrast slip vs. skid stall behavior and tie the skid to base-to-final overshoots [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Brief POH slip and flap limitations and speeds before the lesson; many trainers have specific placards.
gaps: Airplane-specific slip limits (time, fuel quantity, flaps), approach speeds and flap settings come from the POH/AFM; the AFH only says such limits may exist.

Tail stalls with flaps during a slip (PA.IV.M.R7): the resources only say flaps change tail downwash/tail-down force and that slips with flaps may be limited for aerodynamic reasons; no detailed explanation of the slip-induced tail stall mechanism is given (AC 91-74B covers tailplane stall only in icing).
No FAA source here gives a specific procedure for using a slip while being overtaken or for a wind shear encounter in a slip; guidance is drawn from general go-around and wind shear text.
